title: Triple knockdown of CD11a, CD49d, and PSGL1 in T cells reduces CAR-T cell toxicity but preserves activity against solid tumors in mice
source: Science TLDR podcast episode show notes
one_line: shRNA knockdown of three T cell trafficking/adhesion molecules (CD11a, CD49d, PSGL1) in EpCAM-targeted CAR-T cells reduced on-target, off-tumor toxicity in mice while preserving anti-tumor activity.
key_claims: Simultaneous silencing of CD11a, CD49d, and PSGL1 — genes governing T cell extravasation through blood vessel walls into tissues — markedly reduced CAR-T damage to normal EpCAM-expressing tissues.
Triple-knockdown CAR-T cells retained cancer cell killing against EpCAM-positive solid tumors despite impaired tissue infiltration.
Knockdown cells showed reduced tonic signaling and less exhaustion, with enhanced memory formation and better persistence.
Findings were supported using shRNA knockdown plus CRISPR-Cas9 knockout, flow cytometry, immunostaining, and mouse tumor models.
The strategy is proposed as a way to widen the usable CAR target space to antigens like EpCAM that are shared with healthy epithelium.
limitations: In vivo results were less striking than the in vitro findings, and the reasons for that gap were not resolved.
Effects of the tumor microenvironment on the modified cells were not fully characterized.
The approach was not validated across other CAR targets beyond EpCAM.
Work was confined to mouse models; no human/clinical data.
Cost and accessibility of the engineered product remain unaddressed.
open_questions: Does trafficking-molecule knockdown preserve efficacy for other on-target/off-tumor-prone antigens such as HER2?
What mechanism explains the weaker in vivo versus in vitro separation of tumor killing from normal-tissue toxicity?
Can CAR-T cells still enter tumors efficiently long-term if adhesion molecules are silenced rather than transiently suppressed?
